messages.body_plain:
Dear Splusers,

I'd like to ask a detail concerning how many levels an effect should have
before it is permissible/sensible to considered it a random effect:

Douglas Bates wrote:
> Your description of the experimental situation seems to indicate that
> you only have random effects for Location, not for A and B.  In that
> case you would call lme as
>  lme(Y ~ A * B, data = mydata, random = ~ 1)
> but I'm not sure you could make sense of estimating a random effect
> for Location when you only have two different locations.  You may want
> to consider doing a fixed-effects analysis.

(http://wubios.wustl.edu/hyperlists/s-news/200008/msg00286.html)

My problem is that typically in our work (in vitro assay comparisons) we
block experiments by operator, or by laboratory - and we rarely have more
than 3, usually only two. Nevertheless, it would seem desirable that these
kinds of effects are (able to be) considered random. How much of a
constraint is the number of levels on the interpretation of the effect as
random or fixed?

Thanks in advance

Simon Kay

messages.subject: [S] How to separate out overlapping text labels on a plot
messages.subject_clean: [S] How to separate out overlapping text labels on a plot
messages.body_plain:
Dear People of s-news

I would appreciate knowing whether there is any way to avoid text titles on 
a plot from overlapping, and thus rendering them more readable.  For 
example:

lab<-c("test1","test2")
xpoint<-c(0,1)
ypoint<-c(1,0)
plot(xpoint,ypoint)
plot(xpoint,ypoint,xlim=c(0,100),ylim=c(0,20))
plot(xpoint,ypoint,xlim=c(0,100),ylim=c(0,100))
text.default(xpoint, ypoint, labels=lab,col=2,cex=0.7,adj=0)

Produces overlapping labels 'test1' and 'test2'...

I'm dealing with plots with 40 or so lables - some of which overlap.  Does S 
have a separate/(jitter?) option in the par options?  I have been unable to 
find it.  Any guidance would be appreciated...

Thank you kindly
Cello

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-plus users,

I have a question on how to loop through variable names, or names of
datasets. I shall illustrate the problem by way of a small example using
the subset function, contributed by Bradley Biggerstaff.

Example
-------
Data<-as.data.frame(matrix(c(1,11,12,2,11,12,3,22,12,4,22,12,5,12,11),nrow=5
,byrow=T,dimnames=list(NULL,c("a","b","c"))))

Data
     a  b  c 
[1,] 1 11 12
[2,] 2 11 12
[3,] 3 22 12
[4,] 4 22 12
[5,] 5 12 11

# number of rows where a particular variable is equal to a particular level
# no problem !

nrow(subset(Data,b %in% c(11)))

# looping through all levels, and putting the result in "result"
# again no problem !

result<-matrix(nrow=3,ncol=1)
levels<-c(11,12,22)
r<-rank(levels)

for (i in c(levels)) {
j<-r[levels==i]
result[j,]<-nrow(subset(Data,b %in% i))
}

# I did not succeed in looping through variable names

Is this possible ?

Best wishes,

Wouter

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Object names in script
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the long delay in getting this summary out.  I was called away
to other projects.  I haven't had a chance to try out all these
algorithms, but they all look good.  Thanks to all who responded.  Here
goes:

>>From David Brahm and David Smith:

        assign(paste(matrixName, i, sep="."),
        get(paste(matrixName, i, sep=".")) + matrix.c.Stuff)

        I actually did a quick test on this and found that you have to
create the objects and their names      first with the assign function
alone, then in the loop you can use the above algorithm with the get
function.

>>From Hakon Gjessing:

        temp <- vector(mode="list", length=10)

        creates an empty list of length 10. Each element can be 
        accessed, say, with temp[[8]]. You can then store anything you
        want in the list, for instance matrices:

        temp[[5]] <- matrixsomething

        You can also assign names to each element in the list, like

        names(temp) <- c("a", "b", "c" .....etc (character vector of 
        length 10). You can then refer to the first element as
        temp[[1]] or temp[["a"]] or temp$a

>>From Bert Gunter:

        dimnames(MATRIX)[[2]] <- c(dimnames(MATRIX)[[2]],newname)

And from Daniel Hepworth:

        # first example
        # trivial loop to store i in a series of S Plus objects
        # end up with name.1, name.2, ..... name.n

        n<-10
        for (i in 1:n)
        { 
        m<-paste("name.",as.character(i),"<-i",sep="")
        eval(parse(text=m))
        }

        #another example
        for (i in 1:10)
        { 
        temp<-c(pi,i)
        
m<-paste("matrix.name.",as.character(i),"<-matrix(temp,ncol=2)",sep="")
        eval(parse(text=m))
        }

messages.subject: [S] table (factor(...)) with NAs
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I've observed the following behavior from table() on a factor object and
it seems wacky. Can someone tell me whether I'm right in complaining?

Consider the result of c(1, 2, NA, 2, 3). This is a fine-looking vector
which is easy to table:

> table (c(1, 2, NA, 2, 3))
 1 2 3 
 1 2 1

The NA is omitted, but we can get around that with the exclude= option:

> table (c(1, 2, NA, 2, 3), exclude=NULL)
 1 2 3 NA 
 1 2 1  1

Okay. Now suppose that vector is first fed into factor(), and then tabled:

> table (factor (c(1, 2, NA, 2, 3)))
 1 2 3 
 1 2 1

Fair enough. What if I try to get NA's in there, too?

> table (factor (c(1, 2, NA, 2, 3)), exclude=NULL)
 1 2 3 
 1 2 1

Look: no NA's. I can get what I want with an extra as.character(), but I
don't really want to have to. Is this a bug?

Thanks,
Sam ("Table Boy") Buttrey
buttrey at nps.navy.mil

messages.subject: [S] table() with factors
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I strongly agree that the combination of table() with a factor is
a bug; but with the classic "that's not a bug it's a feature" defense
oft mouthed in return.
   Because of the long-term maintainance penalty one must pay for overriding
Splus defaults, I really try to avoid doing so.  But even given this, table()
is one of the two functions that we have globally overridden at Mayo (and we
have 80+ S users).  (The other is as.data.frame.character, preventing the
automatic conversion of character variables into factors).
   Below is our function.

        Terry Therneau
        Section of Biostatistics, Mayo Clinic

----------------------------
.BG
.FN table
.TL
Create Contingency Table from Categories (Mayo modified)
.DN
Returns a contingency table (array)
with the same number of dimensions as arguments given.
.CS
table(..., exclude=NULL)
.RA
.AG ...
any number of objects, each to be interpreted as a
category.
All arguments must be of equal length.
Together, they define a multi-way ragged array of as many dimensions
as there are arguments.
Missing values (`NA's) are allowed.
Arguments that are given in the `name=value' form will have a name in the
dimnames list.
.OA
.AG exclude=
vector of values to exclude from the table.  The standard S default
was NA and NaN, but has been changed locally.
.RT
a multi-way array containing the number of observations in the cells
defined by the arguments to `table'.   For example, if
.Cs
z <- table(arg1, arg2, arg3)
.Ce
then `z[i,j,k]' is the number of times that the combination of the
`i'-th level of the first category, the `j'-th level of the second,
and the `k'-th level of the third appeared together in the data.
A combination is not counted if missing values are present in the corresponding
element of any of the arguments.
.PP
The `dimnames' attribute of the array contains the `levels'
attribute of each of the arguments.
.DT
Returns a multi-way array containing the number of observations in the
cells defined by the arguments to `table'.
.SH Mayo changes
Since table is usually used to display data, NA values are not excluded by
default.
.PP
Factors, dates, and chron objects are handled differently.  Each object in the
argument list is examined using a `tablecut' method.  For date and chron
objects, this method causes the resulting labels to be in character form,
e.g. `10/5/92' instead of `11966'.  For a factor, it ensures that NAs in factor
objects are handled the same way as in other objects.  In the original Splus
function, the inclusion of NA in the table depends on how the factor object was
originally created, ignoring the `exclude' argument of the `table' function
itself.  This behavior is confusing at best.
.PP
Users can add their own tablecut methods for new object classes, or
override the defaults given here without changing the table function itself.
In particular `tablecat.factor <- function(x) x' restores the original
Splus behavior.
.SA
`crosstabs', `cut', `na.include', `factor', `loglin', `tapply', `tabulate', `cat
egory'.
.EX
> Pet <- factor(c("Cat","Dog","Cat","Dog","Cat","?"), exclude="?")
> Food <- factor(c("Dry","Dry","Dry","Wet","Wet","Wet"))
> table(Pet, Food)
    Dry Wet
Cat   2   1
Dog   1   1
.KW category
.WR

---------------
# Differences with Splus:  Don't exclude anything
#    use a "tablecat" method for the categorizing variables
table <-
function(..., exclude = NULL)
{
        if(nargs() == 0)
                stop("No arguments")
        bin <- 0
        lens <- NULL
        dims <- numeric(0)
        pd <- 1
        dn <- list()
        args <- list(...)
        for(i in args) {
                if(is.null(lens))
                        lens <- length(i)
                if(length(i) != lens)
                        stop("All arguments must have the same length")
#               if(!is.category(i))
#                       cat <- category(i, exclude = exclude)
#               else cat <- i
                cat <- tablecat(i, exclude=exclude)
                l <- levels(cat)
                dims <- c(dims, length(l))
                dn <- c(dn, list(l))
                bin <- bin + pd * (as.numeric(cat) - 1)
                pd <- pd * length(l)
        }
        names(dn) <- names(args)
        bin <- bin[!is.na(bin)]
        array(tabulate(bin + 1, pd), dims, dn)
}

----------------------
#SCCS @(#)tablecat.s    1.2 10/4/95
tablecat <- function(x, ...)
    UseMethod("tablecat")

tablecat.default <- function(x, exclude)
    category(x, exclude=exclude)

tablecat.factor <- function(x, exclude) {
    if (any(is.na(x))) {
        newlev <- unique(c(levels(x), NA))
        newlev <- newlev[is.na(match(newlev, exclude))]
        newx <- match(x, newlev)
        levels(newx) <- newlev
        newx
        }
    else x
    }

tablecat.date <- function(x, exclude) {
   category(as.character(x), exclude=exclude)
   }

tablecat.chron <- function(x, exclude)
   category(format(x), exclude=exclude)

messages.subject: [S] Re: Data mining comparison
messages.body_plain:
> Date: Wed, 30 Aug 2000 14:14:48 +0100
> From: Peter England <peter.england at emb.co.uk>
> Subject: [S] Data mining comparison
>
> Does anyone know of a paper/web site etc which compares data mining
> techniques e.g GLMs, neural nets, CARTs, Bayes Nets etc.?
>
> Note: I am aware of Brian Ripley's SDM library and the rpart library - I
am
> interested in comparisons of the techniques - pros and cons, preferably
with
> examples carried out on the same data set.

If you are talking about the statistical classification or supervised
learning
aspect of the data mining enterprise, there are two important references
which
happen to be listed in Part 1 of the Neural Network FAQ.

1.  The on-line book "Machine Learning Neural and Statistical
Classification", by
     Michie D, Speigelhalter DJ, and Taylor C, which is a report of the
     ESPRIT Statlog project.

2.  The paper "A Comparison of Prediction Accuracy, Complexity, and
     Training Thirty-Three Old and New Classification Algorithms" by
     Lim, Loh, and Shih.

The Lim paper has quite a few references to S-Plus.  Some of the data sets
used
in the ESPRIT project are held in the Machine Learning archive at UC Irvine.
However,
the data sets which show clear differences in performance - credit, power
stability - are
proprietary and not generally available.

You can easily trace down all these references using a search engine -
www.google.com
is the current champion.

There have been quite a few papers published by the academic community
(Poggio,
Ripley, Bishop, Sarle etc.) which have the general theme that the
performance
of all these methods is similar, and that in particular, neural networks are
really just
function approximation or regularization, or regression - nonlinear,
logistic,
projection pursuit, ridge, etc. etc.  However, I find the literature on the
entire subject
of classification methodologies, both from the statistical and computer
science -
artificial intelligence communities to suffer from a variety of fundamental
weaknesses,
beginning with Fisher's original example of the Iris taxonomic(?) data.

The bottom line is that while there are now an enormous range of tools to
carry out these
tasks, it is still not clear how to select tools and carry out a
classification task while
insuring statistical rigor (outliers, overfitting etc.).  Because neural
networks have
been claimed to offer superior performance on several tasks of interest to
molecular biologists (e.g. protein folding - Rost EMBL) I have decided, as
much for own amusement, to see if it would be possible to find alternative
approaches
which would be based on a sounder analysis of fundamentals than those
typically found
in the literature.

Note, I am not the Alan J. Robinson of the European Bioinformatics Institute
(EBI)

Alan J. Robinson
robin073 at tc.umn.edu

received two suggestions.

messages.body_plain:
There are two positons available here in the Tropical and Pelagic
Ecosystems Program at the CSIRO Marine Research Laboratories,
Cleveland, Queensland, Australia.  The official ads appeared in
the 2nd September edition of "The Australian" newspaper.

Position 1: Population Dynamics and Stock Assessment Modeller.
Contact for details: Cathy.Dichmont at marine.csiro.au (or me).

Position 2: Spatial Analyst and Modeller for Marine, Coastal,
         Estuarine and Riparian Ecosystems.  
Contact for details: Francis.Pantus at marine.csiro.au (or me).

For both positions our requirements are fairly open.  We are
basically looking for flexible, qualified and experienced people
in population dynamics or stock assessment models (position 1) or
spatial analysis and spatial models (position 2), or in closely
allied areas, preferably in the marine ecosystem context.

These are relatively senior research positions with substantial
responsibilities and challenges, both in sensitive ecosystem
research and in management support and strategy evaluation.

The current intention is for both positions to be line-managed by
me.  Although they are in the CSIRO Marine Research Division
(CMR) position 2 and to a lesser extent position 1 will also
have substantial interactions with the CSIRO Mathematical and
Information Sciences Division (CMIS), to which I belong.

We would be grateful if you would draw this notice to the
attention of any potentially interested applicants.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Object names in script
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the long delay in getting this summary out.  I was called away
to other projects.  I haven't had a chance to try out all these
algorithms, but they all look good.  Thanks to all who responded.  Here
goes:

>>From David Brahm and David Smith:

        assign(paste(matrixName, i, sep="."),
        get(paste(matrixName, i, sep=".")) + matrix.c.Stuff)

        I actually did a quick test on this and found that you have to
create the objects and their names      first with the assign function
alone, then in the loop you can use the above algorithm with the get
function.

>>From Hakon Gjessing:

	temp <- vector(mode="list", length=10)

        creates an empty list of length 10. Each element can be
        accessed, say, with temp[[8]]. You can then store anything you
        want in the list, for instance matrices:

	temp[[5]] <- matrixsomething

	You can also assign names to each element in the list, like

        names(temp) <- c("a", "b", "c" .....etc (character vector of
        length 10). You can then refer to the first element as
        temp[[1]] or temp[["a"]] or temp$a

>>From Bert Gunter:

	dimnames(MATRIX)[[2]] <- c(dimnames(MATRIX)[[2]],newname)

And from Daniel Hepworth:

        # first example
        # trivial loop to store i in a series of S Plus objects
        # end up with name.1, name.2, ..... name.n

        n<-10
        for (i in 1:n)
        {
        m<-paste("name.",as.character(i),"<-i",sep="")
        eval(parse(text=m))
        }

        #another example
        for (i in 1:10)
        {
        temp<-c(pi,i)
        
m<-paste("matrix.name.",as.character(i),"<-matrix(temp,ncol=2)",sep="")
        eval(parse(text=m))
        }

messages.subject: [S] Re: Data mining comparison
messages.body_plain:
> Date: Wed, 30 Aug 2000 14:14:48 +0100
> From: Peter England <peter.england at emb.co.uk>
> Subject: [S] Data mining comparison
>
> Does anyone know of a paper/web site etc which compares data mining
> techniques e.g GLMs, neural nets, CARTs, Bayes Nets etc.?
>
> Note: I am aware of Brian Ripley's SDM library and the rpart library - I
am
> interested in comparisons of the techniques - pros and cons, preferably
with
> examples carried out on the same data set.

If you are talking about the statistical classification or supervised
learning
aspect of the data mining enterprise, there are two important references
which
happen to be listed in Part 1 of the Neural Network FAQ.

1.  The on-line book "Machine Learning Neural and Statistical
Classification", by
     Michie D, Speigelhalter DJ, and Taylor C, which is a report of the
     ESPRIT Statlog project.

2.  The paper "A Comparison of Prediction Accuracy, Complexity, and
     Training Thirty-Three Old and New Classification Algorithms" by
     Lim, Loh, and Shih.

The Lim paper has quite a few references to S-Plus.  Some of the data sets
used
in the ESPRIT project are held in the Machine Learning archive at UC Irvine.
However,
the data sets which show clear differences in performance - credit, power
stability - are
proprietary and not generally available.

You can easily trace down all these references using a search engine -
www.google.com
is the current champion.

There have been quite a few papers published by the academic community
(Poggio,
Ripley, Bishop, Sarle etc.) which have the general theme that the
performance
of all these methods is similar, and that in particular, neural networks are
really just
function approximation or regularization, or regression - nonlinear,
logistic,
projection pursuit, ridge, etc. etc.  However, I find the literature on the
entire subject
of classification methodologies, both from the statistical and computer
science -
artificial intelligence communities to suffer from a variety of fundamental
weaknesses,
beginning with Fisher's original example of the Iris taxonomic(?) data.

The bottom line is that while there are now an enormous range of tools to
carry out these
tasks, it is still not clear how to select tools and carry out a
classification task while
insuring statistical rigor (outliers, overfitting etc.).  Because neural
networks have
been claimed to offer superior performance on several tasks of interest to
molecular biologists (e.g. protein folding - Rost EMBL) I have decided, as
much for own amusement, to see if it would be possible to find alternative
approaches
which would be based on a sounder analysis of fundamentals than those
typically found
in the literature.

Note, I am not the Alan J. Robinson of the European Bioinformatics Institute
(EBI)

Alan J. Robinson
robin073 at tc.umn.edu

messages.subject: Re: [S] Advice on lme formula construction - random or fixed effects??
messages.subject_clean: [S] Advice on lme formula construction - random or fixed effects??
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus group,

Thanks to the quick response to my question:

> > My problem is that typically in our work (in vitro assay comparisons) we
> > block experiments by operator, or by laboratory - and we rarely have
more
> > than 3, usually only two. Nevertheless, it would seem desirable that
these
> > kinds of effects are (able to be) considered random. How much of a
> > constraint is the number of levels on the interpretation of the effect
as
> > random or fixed?

from the five below (presented in no particular order). The answer is
straightforward - be careful sampling with too few levels since the
reliability of the estimates of variance compnents will suffer. But it also
seems clear to me the choice is one of the experimental design, i.e. what
information is to be extracted from the experiment, and the types of
conclusions that you wish to reach (so in my case, it becomes important to
consider labs and operators as random effects).

Thanks again to all.

Simon

----- Original Message -----
From: "A.J. Rossini" <rossini at blindglobe.net>
> Random effects are used for situations when the number of levels of
> the factor is unknown.  If you know that there are only 3 possible
> (whatevers), then it's a fixed effect.  However, if it's from a
> population of whatevers, where you have no way of ever choosing k
> levels, then it's random.  Worse, if you only have 3 whatevers, and
> you choose to call it a random effect, it "sounds" like a poor design,
> since it sounds like you have a fixed population.
>
> best,
> -tony
>
> --
> A.J. Rossini Rsrch. Asst. Prof. of Biostatistics
> BlindGlobe Networks (home/default) rossini at blindglobe.net
> UW Biostat/Center for AIDS Research rossini at biostat.washington.edu
> FHCRC/SCHARP/HIV Vaccine Trials Net rossini at scharp.org

----- Original Message -----
From: "Albyn Jones" <jones at reed.edu>
> The distinction is not based on how many levels there are, but on
> whether you have all levels of interest represented in the experiment
> or just a sample of the levels.  If you have a sample of the
> population of levels, and wish to generalize to the population from
> the sample, then it is correct to treat it as a random effect -
> even if there are only a finite number of levels in the population.
>
> Years ago I read a paper by Tukey discussing the details, and
> I could probably find a reference if necessary.
>
> It sounds to me that your real worry should be the reliability of
> estimating a variance component based on 1 or 2 df.
>
> albyn
> ------------------------------------------------------------------
> http://www.reed.edu/~jones    Albyn Jones   jones at reed.edu
> Reed College, Portland OR 97202             (503)-771-1112 x7418

----- Original Message -----
From: James Roger <James at livedata.co.uk>
Well, the crucial question is why do you want to treat the factor as a
random effect. From this one can address the implications.

For instance:
1. Want to get wide inferences (allow for higher stratum level variability)
in adjusted means. Similarly for treatment differences when including a
treatment-by-centre (say) interaction.

2. To recover between block information in incomplete block designs.

In case 1 you might treat it as random even with very small numbers, but the
s.e. would be poorly estimated. This would be seen in the very few
denominator degrees of freedom for and confidence interval based on t and
Satherthwaite style d.f.s

In case 2 it would be safer to do a fixed effects analysis. An alternative
if there was a lot of between block information would be to add some prior
information about the ratio of between to within block variability.

Hope that this helps.

James.

----- Original Message -----
From: "Andrew Robinson" <andrewr at uidaho.edu>

> the difference between a fixed and a random effect in this context is
> that the estimates of fixed effects are of interest in themselves,
> whereas random effects are like a sample that represents a
> population, and it is the population that is of interest.  Therefore
> in this case there would be a sample of size n=2.  In the case of
> taper in trees (!) the diameter is the response variable, the height
> of the measurements would be a fixed effect, and the tree number
> would be a random effect, as the trees are a random sample from the
> population.  2 is a very small sample size for an effect of interest.
> But if that's all you have, and it's definitely not fixed, then go
> for it.
>

> --
> Andrew

----- Original Message -----
From: "Jim Pratt" <JimP at sonuspharma.com>

Simon,

If there are a few levels of a random factor, then it does not penalized you
a great deal to estimate as fixed, you loss of error DF is minimal.  When
there are a large number of levels, then to fit as fixed effects typically
reduces the error DF substantially.  therefore, random effects are nice
since you can reduce the number of parameters to just a few, not k-1
(k=number of levels for random effect).

Also with few levels of a random effect, one would expect to obtain poor
estimates of its variance component.  I think the fixed effects would pretty
much best estimated the same, either way.  So why go through the hassle of
mixed effects modeling when you most likely will not gain much.

When you mention you random effect is operator or laboratory, are these the
only ones you will use or are they truly a random sample of potential
operators/labs?  What are you trying to say about operator/lab?  Do you need
to estimate anything about them, or are you basically trying to account for
them in the model?  If trying to estimate their variance components, then
probably need more than a few levels to do a reasonable job.  If trying to
account for them in the analysis, I believe you'll get the same answer it
treat them as fixed effects (and a much easier time doing it).

James Pratt

Addendum:

I should like to add to my previous post that this is a very large and
active research field, complete with numerous controversies, and that there
are some new methodologies in active development which don't appear in the
Michie and Lim references I gave.  While there is some software available on
the Internet to try out these methods, I didn't find any mention of
implementations in standard statistical packages such as S-Plus.  It remains
to be seen whether these methodologies will find wide spread use, but if the
researchers claims of superior performance are substantiated, they have the
potential for introducing major philosophical changes and perspectives into
this field.

Some of the more intriguing methods include Support Vector Machines, kernel
density estimation, and gaussian processes.  They often make use of
mathematical methods such as Hilbert spaces and Riemannian metrics commonly
used in other disciplines such as physics, but not often seen in statistics.
They also make use of distinctively Russian mathematical research into such
topics as functional approximation.  For me there is a personal irony in
this as I used a theorem of Serge Bernstein's from the Russian mathematical
literature in my bachelor's thesis many years ago, and felt that this work
and its emphasis on generalized function approximation had significant
potential and deserved wider appreciation in the West.

Alan J. Robinson

messages.subject: [S] lowess and loess function differences
messages.body_plain:
Here are the responses I received regarding differences between lowess and 
loess.

Thank you.

At least three differences:
1) lowess uses local linear regression, loess (by default) local quadratic.
2) by default, loess does not do robustness iterations.
3) both use direct evaluation at a reduced set of points, followed by
   interpolation. But the algorithms are different: lowess uses linear
   interpolation; loess cubic interpolation from a coarser set of points.

***********************************

One obvious place is the robust fitting:  lowess goes through iterations to
down-weight points with large residuals.  loess, by default, don't.  If you
specify family='symmetric' in loess, the result will be much closer.  If you
sum the absolute differences between the two, you will get something around
0.83.  Adding the family='symmetric' argument to loess brings that down to
0.07.

***************************************************************

There are a number of differences in the parameter settings for the two
procedures. For examples, lowess() has a "delta" parameter that loess()
doesn't -- loess() uses its "subset" parameter for the same purpose, but the
defaults (which you used) are different. lowess() does robust fitting only;
loess() can, but it's default is not to (which you used). Etc. ...

What would be interesting to see is if you did set up the calls to give
identical results, would they? I haven't tried, but let us know what happens
if and when you do.

**************************************************************************

messages.body_plain:
All,

I have been calculating autocorrelations by brute force because I have
missing data.  I calculate lags and use ts.union to put everything in a
time series table (data class: rts) with this algorithm:

        for (i in 0:24)
        {
                l.cats.ts <- lag(COF.cats.lag, -i)
                TTS.COF.cats.lag <- ts.union(TTS.COF.cats.lag,
l.cats.ts)
        }
 
In order to manipulate the data, I found I had to change the rts into a
data.frame with the command

        Cool.TTS.COF.cats.lag <- data.frame(TTS.COF.cats.lag)

I want to use table() to count the number of pairs between 2 columns in
the new data.frame.  When I use the command (using columns 1 and 3 as an
example), I get the table followed by 2 warning messages:

> table(Cool.TTS.COF.cats.lag$TTS.COF.cats.lag.1,
Cool.TTS.COF.cats.lag$TTS.COF.cats.lag.3)
    1  2  3  4    5 
1 263 31 35 17  200
2  37 34 19 10   40
3  22 12 23 13   24

Warning messages:

partial))

partial))

The table is exactly what I want, but the warning messages play havoc

messages.subject: [S] Text Positioning in S-Plus 2000
messages.body_plain:
S-Plus 2000 with SR 3, running on Win 2000 with SP 1.

Automatic text positioning in graphsheets is imperfect.  In some
cases, text is positioned too low.  This makes the last line of text
in a key (created with "key") run into the border, and the same
effect seems to happen in Trellis plots, where the strip text runs into
the bottom of the strip.  This is most evident when Type 1 fonts are
used.  I do remember from non-S similar problems that Type 1 fonts
are positioned lower in the character cell than some others, which
contributes to this.

A related question is why "legend" sometimes puts a huge amount
of whitespace around a legend.  The following code snippet resulted
in overly wide right and left margins within the legend border:

leg.names <- c("Main trajectory","Alternative
traj.")

legend(1977,1.0),leg.names,marks=c(1,2))

I tried to improve the result by specifying two corners for the legend,
but the material inside was still not centered and was rendered with a
wide margin on the left and ran into the legend border on the 
right.

Any suggestions will be welcomed, as will comments on whether this is
improved in the upcoming version of S-Plus.

-- 

Michael Prager

Beaufort, North Carolina  28516  USA

messages.subject: [S] Summary: ROC curve
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Many thanks to those who provided valuable advice.  Here is my original
question and a summary of response.

Thanks once again.

Ly-Mee

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
^^^^
Question:
  > I like to carry out an internal validation (using bootstrap method) for
my
> logistic model after a stepwise approach.  One of the calculations is the
> area under ROC curve for each bootstrap sample.  Does S-plus have any
> function(s) to calculate area of a ROC curve?  Anyway advice is much
> approaciated.
>
 > Thanks

Responses:
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

The validate function in the Design library, when used on fits
 from lrm (also from Design) will validate Somers' Dxy rank
 correlation, which is 2(C-.5) where C=ROC area.
 Design is built-in to S+ 2000, and must also be used with
the Hmisc library.  For other versions of S+ you can get
 the software from our web page (see below).  validate will
 do bootstrap or cross-validation.

 The Hmisc library has a little function for computing ROC
 area (somers2).

-Frank Harrell

+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Check out http://www.mayo.edu/hsr/Sfunc.html to find the roc functions that
I wrote w/ Doug Mahoney.

- Beth

 =====================================================================
Beth Atkinson                                  (507) 284-0431
 Mayo Clinic                                    (507) 284-9542  FAX
 200 First Street SW
 Rochester, MN  55905                           atkinson at mayo.edu
 =====================================================================

 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Here is my "home-made" function. It seems to work reasonably well.

 roc
function(x, bh, wgts = rep(1, length(x)), x0 = x)
{
#x may be a vector of x-values, or may be a matrix
#   of x-values, the points at which p is evaluated.
# Let mu = x bh, where 1 has been added to the beginning
# of x to accomodate the constant term. bh is the vector
#of coefficients usually obtained using glm. If x is a
# vector then bh must have length 2. If x is a matrix then
# the the length of bh must be equal to the number of columns
#of x after adding the column of ones.
# We assume that p(x[i,]) = 1/(1+exp(-mu)).
#The result is a list. The first element is A, the area under
#the ROC curve, using a rectangular method. The second elemen
t
# is an estimate of Var(A). The third element is a matrix of
# values with columns R and H which are estimates of P(+| D)=

# Sensitivity and P(+ | not-D) =  1 - Specificity . The ROC
# may be plotted using this matrix.
# Usually the x-points used to determine (R, H) are the eleme
nts of
# x. However they need not be. In that case use x0 instead.
         X0 <- cbind(1, x0)
         x <- rep(x, wgts)
         mu <- c(cbind(1, x) %*% bh)
         mu <- sort(mu)
         mu0 <- c(cbind(1, x0) %*% bh)
         mu0 <- sort(mu0)
         n <- length(mu0)
         p <- 1/(1 + exp( - mu))
         q <- 1 - p
         p0 <- 1/(1 + exp( - mu0))
         q0 <- 1 - p0
         B <- outer(mu0, mu0, "<=")
         R <- c(B %*% p0)
         R <- R/R[1]
         H <- c(B %*% (1 - p0))
         H <- H/H[1]
         B <- outer(p0, 1 - p0)
         den <- sum(p0) * sum(q0)
         A <- sum(B * outer(1:n, 1:n, "<="))/den
         X <- cbind(1, x)
         Q <- outer(p0, q0) * (1 - outer(q0, p0, "-")) *
                 outer(1:n, 1:n, "<=")
         a <- apply(t(Q) %*% X0, 2, sum)
         M <- t(X) %*% diag(p * q) %*% X
         MI <- solve(M)
         V <- (1/den^2) * t(a) %*% MI %*% matrix(a)
         list(A, V, cbind(R, H))
}

Jim Stapleton
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Hi

You can find some infos on this matter on the s-archives:

 http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-archive/199902/msg00100.html

but I would be interested by the more recent answers you will get on
this matter.

Here are below two functions that I wrote myself to calculate AUC from a
ROC plot, but they are probably not the most elegant solutions !

 ****************** roc.plot function *****************************
  source("d:\\s_lib\\newfunc\\rocplot.fun")
 # Fonction roc.plot written by Antoine Guisan (Swiss Center for Faunal
 Cartography, 1999)
 # See table 2 in Fielding & Bell (1997), Environmental Conservation
 24(1): 41
 # se = sensitivity, sp = specificity; make use of the roc.plot.auc
 function
 # z1 = vector of predicted values between 0 and 1; z2 = vector of
 observed values 0/1
 roc.plot_function(z1, z2)
 {
 eva <- data.frame()
 eva[1,"seuil"] <- 0
 eva[1,"se"] <- 1
 eva[1,"sp"] <- 0
 k <- 0.01
 i <- 2
 while(k < 0.9) {
 a <- table(z1 >= k, z2)[4]
 b <- table(z1 >= k, z2)[2]
 c <- table(z1 >= k, z2)[3]
 d <- table(z1 >= k, z2)[1]
 eva[i,"seuil"] <- k
 eva[i,"se"] <- ifelse(a / (a + c) == "NA", 0, a / (a + c))
 eva[i,"sp"] <- d / (b + d)
 k <- k + 0.01
 i <- i + 1
 }
 eva[i,"seuil"] <- 1
 eva[i,"se"] <- 0
 eva[i,"sp"] <- 1
 return(list(data = eva, auc = 1 + roc.plot.auc(eva)))
 }

 ********************* roc.plot.auc function *******************************
 # ROC.PLOT.AUC function to calculate the 'Area Under the Curve'
 # as defined in the ROC-Plot methodology (see Fielding & Bell 1997)
 # written by XXX xxx
 # source("d:\\s_lib\\newfunc\\rocplotauc.fun")

.auc<-function(x){      
 X<-data.frame(sens=x$se,spec=x$sp,eenminspec=1-x$sp,
                         diffsens=rep(0,length=length(x$se)),
                         diffspec=rep(0,length=length(x$sp)),
                         area=rep(0,length=length(x$se)))
       
 X$diffsens[-(nrow(x))]<-X$sens[2:(nrow(X))]-X$sens[1:(nrow(X)-1)]
 
 X$diffspec[-(nrow(x))]<-X$eenminspec[2:(nrow(X))]-X$eenminspec[1:(nrow(X)-1)]
         X$area<-X$sens*X$diffspec+0.5*X$diffsens*X$diffspec
         return(sum(X$area))
 }

Antoine Guisan

+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

 for the R
OC you can use the lrm function in Frank Harrell's Hmisc library

 Harrell's library also have a number of bootstrap functions available, -
 check the HMISC help files.

 Have fun!

Thanks again to Bill Dunlap and Shawn Boles for coming up with a quick
solution to my problem.  Here is Bill's explanation of why I was getting
the warnings:

You get the warnings because table is subscripting its arguments
and when you subscript a time series the result is not generally
a time series (e.g., if you scramble its elements it is not a time
series any more). 

Both Shawn and Bill pointed out that I can get rid of the warnings with
options(warn=-1) since the warnings did not affect the output I needed.
Bill also suggested that I could change the columns to numeric vectors
from numeric time series using something like

        data[] <- lapply(data, as.numeric)

messages.subject: Re: [S] Sampling correlated vectors
messages.body_plain:
Mark Tardiff writes:

>  I have two variables, X and Y,  that are correlated (r=0.7).  I have
>  created empirical density distributions for X and Y using the density
>  function.  I want to take a random sample of X and then sample Y, such that
>  the sampled values of X and Y will be correlated with r=0.7.

This is I think a fairly cute question; it is also somewhat ill-posed.

Essentially what you want to do is choose a sample

        (x_1^*, y_1^*), ... (x_n^*, y_n^*)

from amongst all pairs (x_i, y_j) of x and y values from the existing sample.
(The existing sample being (x_1,y_1), ..., (x_n,y_n).

The size of your ``re-sample'' need not necessarily be the same as
the original sample size --- but it is in bootstrapping procedures
which is presumably what you have in mind.

You want to do this in such a way that the correlation of the
{(x_i^*,y_i^*)} sample is r = 0.7.  If by this you mean that you want
the ***sample*** correlation of the {(x_i^*,y_i^*)} sample to equal
0.7, then you are attempting the impossible (and the silly).  What
you ***should*** mean is that you want the theoretical correlation of
your sampling procedure to be rho = 0.7.  (So that the long run average
correlation of you bootstrap samples is 0.7.)

So what you really have is the following problem:

        Define a discrete bivariate distribution of random variables
        X and Y, with marginal values x_1, ..., x_n, and y_1, ..., y_n
        so that

                1) the marginal probabilities are all 1/n

                2) the individual cell probabilities are such
                   that the correlation between X and Y is rho = 0.7.

        (This assumes that the values x_1, ..., x_n are all distinct,
        and like wise for the y_1, ..., y_n.)

        More explicitly --- let the cell probabilities be p_ij.
        Without loss of generality assume that

                 n                 n
                SUM x_i = 0   and SUM y_i = 0
                i=1               i=1

        and

              1   n                     1   n
             --- SUM x_i^2 = 1   and   --- SUM y_i^2 = 1
              n  i=1                    n  i=1

        (i.e. make the marginal means 0 and the marginal population
         variances 1.  The x and y values can be rescaled so that
         this is so.)

        Then you want:

                 n
           (c1) SUM p_ij = 1/n for all i, and
                j=1

                 n
           (c2) SUM p_ij = 1/n for all j, and
                i=1

                 n   n
           (c3) SUM SUM x_i y_j p_ij = rho = 0.7
                i=1 j=1

        This is a problem with n^2 - 1 free variables (the p_ij) and
        2(n-1) + 1 constraints.  So it should have lots of
        solutions.  Does it?  Well an approximate solution would be
        just to make p_ij = 1/n for the cells corresponding to the
        original observations, and 0 elsewhere.  (So you have exactly
        1 non-zero p_ij in each row and each column.)  This actually
        gives rho = n*0.7/(n-1) because of the descrepancy between
        sample and population variances, but it's clear that you can
        at least get close.  What you're then doing is of course just
        taking a bootstrap sample from the original sample
        {(x_1,y_1), ..., (x_n,y_n)}.  But this is presumably
        ***not*** what you want.

        It seems pretty clear that there are a gazillion exact
        solutions.  This is where the ill-posed-ness comes in.

        To make the question well-posed, a further condition --- or
        further conditions --- must be applied.

        One vague condition that is intuitively appealing is to make
        the joint distribution as close to uniform as possible.  A couple
        of ways of making this condition precise are

                              n   n
                (A) minimize SUM SUM (p_ij - 1/n^2)^2
                             i=1 j=1

                subject to the constraints c1, c2, and c3.

                                             n   n
                (B) maximize the entropy -[ SUM SUM p_ij ln p_ij ]
                                            i=1 j=1

                subject to the constraints c1, c2, and c3.

        These should I think be fairly tractible OR/linear programming
        type optimization problems.

messages.subject: [S] un-stacking a ragged array
messages.body_plain:
Hi S-gurus,

It is often the case that different data structures are more convenient
for different types of anlaysis. Since I use Trellis a great deal, I
tend to keep my data in 'stacked' format, so that I have a single
response column and a set of columns identifying the 'design variables.'

Sometimes, however, it is useful to make a 'wide' format, where you take
the response vector and cut it up according to one or more of the design
variables and create a new matrix with N columns, where N is the number
of levels in the design variable which you used.

If there are equal numbers of instances for all levels of the design
variable, then this is very easy. I wrote a function to do this long ago
and the PC version of Splus now has an un-stack function.

However, if there are un-equal instances of for each level of the design
variable, then I don't know an elegant solution for creating a complete
array containing all instances and having either "NA's" or something
else in the spots for missing data.

For instance a typical case might be as follows:

> wafer   bin     Fails
> 1       29      6
> 1       33      2
> 1       54      4
> 1       66      6
> 2       29      98
> 2       44      2
> 2       54      6
> 2       69      4
>

and I want to get something like the following:

> wafer   bin29   bin33   bin44   bin54   bin66   bin69
> 1       6       2       NA      4       6       NA
> 2       98      NA      2       6       NA      4
>
Does someone out there have an elegant/fast solution for this?

Thanks for any and all help!

regards,
jcd

messages.subject: Re: [S] uncertainities from ratios
messages.body_plain:
Mario,

I happen to have a canned answer to your question about uncertainty
of the ratio, from a previous e-mail query (not on s-news).  I've
expressed the answer in terms of the coefficient of variation
(ratio of standard error to mean) for the ratio of two variables,
A, B, since that comes out in a fairly simple form.

I attach the material below.  The general principle (using Taylor's
series as shown) applies to other nonlinear combinations of
variables.  The method works only when the coefficient of
variation is fairly small, which is true in the numerical
examples that you mention in your query.  You should be able to
use Equation 3 below.

Dave Krantz

        ------start of attached material------

What is the relation between the standard errors of A, B,
and that of the ratio A/B?

The Taylor series for  R = A/B,  through its first two orders,
looks like this:

dR ~ (1/B)*dA - (A/B^2)*dB + (A/B^3)*dB^2 - (1/B^2)*dA*dB       (EQ 1)

(there is no term for dA^2 since the second partial derivative of R
with respect to A is 0).
In the application here, dA and dB can be considered independent
random variables with mean 0 (departures of sample mean from population
mean for the two samples--it is important that the samples are
independent, of course).

If one squares EQ 1, takes expectations, uses independence and mean 0,
and simplifies, one gets the following second-order approximation,
in which cvA, cvB, and cvR denote the coefficients of variation
of A, B, and R, B3 denotes the normalized third central moment
of the denominator B (expectation of the third power of the deviation
from the mean, divided by the third power of the mean), and B4 denotes
the analogous normalized fourth central moment of B:

cvR ~ sqrt(cvA^2 + cvB^2 + (cvA*cvB)^2 - 2*B3 + B4)             (EQ 2)

If the central limit theorem applies approximately to statistic B,
so its distribution is approximately Gaussian, EQ 2 can be simplified:
B3 is essentially 0 and B4 is approximately 3*(cvB^4).  So for this case,
the second-order approximation becomes

cvR ~ sqrt(cvA^2 + cvB^2 + (cvA*cvB)^2 + 3*(cvB^4))             (EQ 3)

If cvA and cvB are less than 20%, this is a quite good approximation;
and if they are less than 10%, the latter two terms in it play little
role--the first order approximation, essentially Pythagorean combination
of coefficients of variation is pretty good.  However, this second-order
approximation goes to pot rapidly for coefficients of variation
over 20%--one needs higher terms of the Taylor expansion and it
may no longer be worthwhile to look for any formula unless you have
particularly interesting special cases.

        ------end of attached material------

Can I add a follow up question to the thread on the values in Table 2.2
of Davidian & Giltinan.

The values for the GLS, Theta=1 1 row of Table 2.2 can be obtained using
gnls as follows:
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> gnls(data = indoid5, model = Conc ~ (exp(beta1) * exp( - Time *
exp(beta2)) + 
        exp(beta3) * exp( - Time * exp(beta4))), start = list(beta1 = 1,
beta2
         = 1, beta3 = -1, beta4 = -1), weights = varPower(fixed = 1))

  Model: Conc ~ (exp(beta1) * exp( - Time * exp(beta2)) + exp(beta3) *
exp( - Time *   exp(beta4)))

Coefficients:

 1.214251 0.9500488 -1.454529 -1.770808

 power 
     1

Residual standard error: 0.1716829 
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

I then tried doing the calculation using the general nlmin function
calculating the likelihood as follows
The first four parameters xx[1] to xx[4] are beta1 to beta4 as in D&G
notation. pred is mu-hat the predicted value based on the current
estimate of the beta parameters. xx[5] is the current estimate of the
sigma-squared parameter. SS is the variance for each observation. 

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> f2 <- function(xx)
{
        pred <- exp(xx[1]) * exp( - exp(xx[2]) * indoid5$Time) +
exp(xx[3]) * 
                exp( - exp(xx[4]) * indoid5$Time)
        SS <- max(xx[5], 1e-005) * pred * pred
        sum(log(SS) + ((indoid5$Conc - pred)^2)/SS)
}
> start2 <- c(1, 1, -1, -1, 0.1)
> nlmin(f = f2, x = start2, max.iter = 50, max.fcal = 200)      
$x:
[1]  1.1923429  0.9439722 -1.4396035 -1.7560121  0.0187007

$converged:
[1] T

$conv.type:
[1] "relative function convergence"
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

I then tried the same thing using the profile likelihood profiling out
the sigma-squared parameter as explained in section 7.5.1 of Panheiro
and Bates.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> f3 <- function(xx)
{
        pred <- exp(xx[1]) * exp( - exp(xx[2]) * indoid5$Time) +
exp(xx[3]) * 
                exp( - exp(xx[4]) * indoid5$Time)
        N <- sum(indoid5$Conc > 0)      # print(xx)
        N * log(sum(((indoid5$Conc - pred)/pred)^2)/N) + sum(log(pred *
pred))
}
> start3 <- c(1, 1, -1, -1)
> nlmin(f = f3, x = start3, max.iter = 50, max.fcal = 200)      
        # Note that a single cylce of gnls moves it away from our
solution
$x:
[1]  1.1923428  0.9439723 -1.4396036 -1.7560123

$converged:
[1] T

$conv.type:
[1] "relative function convergence"
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
Which gets me the same answer as before.

Can anyone please explain where my theory has gone wrong? I have been
going around and round in circles on this one. I am presumably doing
something wrong/different.

I only did this to clarify things in my own mind. Now I am more
confused.

James.

messages.subject: [S] SAS does; S-Plus doesn't
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Before I forget, I am using S-Plus 2000, Release 2 on a 300mHz Pentium with
64 Mg RAM.

I have two issues which I encountered while modeling some soil degradation
data.  The first related to nls and why S-Plus doesn't converge when SAS
PROC NLIN does.  The second issue is, perhaps, a more philosophical question
related to setting intercepts.

1)  I have about twenty data sets of soil degradation data, each with 5 to
10 data points.  The response is percent remaining where the response has
been scaled such that at time zero 100% remains and covariate is days .
Some of the degradation curves exhibit classic first-order decay patterns of
roughly exponential decline.  Others exhibit nearly linear decay patterns.
To each data set I have been fitting a series of possible models, including
exponential and biexponential models.  Three of the data sets in question
are presented below.

# linear profile
days.1 <- c(0,28,56,84,161)
pct.1 <- c(100,64.89,59.19,48.71,23.90)
# linear profile
days.2 <- c(0,7,14,21,30,43)
pct.2 <- c(100,81.8,67.9,69.2,40,8.61)
# exponential decline
days.3 <- c(0,3,7,14,21,28,56,129,224,357)
pct.3 <- c(100,67.76,74.59,55.09,35.1,24.38,15.11,5.85,3.41,2.44)

# modeling statements for 3-parameter biexponential model, intercept forced
through 100 at days=0
ex1.nls <- nls(pct.1 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.1) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.1),
trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005),nls.control(minscale=.0001,maxiter=100
,tolerance=.1))
ex2.nls <- nls(pct.2 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.2) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.2),
trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005),nls.control(minscale=.0001,maxiter=100
,tolerance=.1))
ex3.nls <- nls(pct.3 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.3) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.3),
trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005))

[Note that the error messages for the first two models differ.  exp1.nls
fails with "singular gradient matrix" (understandable) and exp2.nls fails
with "step factor reduced below minimum".]

 I was not surprised to find that nls did not converge on the first two
sets, since to model this rather linear data using a biexponential model is
to invite problems.  However, I was somewhat surprised to find that SAS's
PROC NLIN did fit these models without difficulty.  Since this is an
academic exercise and not an analysis for a client I am not overly
concerned.  Still, I do find it disturbing that a colleague with essentially
no experience with nonlinear models can code an inappropriate model into SAS
and get convergence whereas I, using S-Plus and the same model description
and starting values (simply double-checking his results), fail to get
convergence.  Would someone with more experience using nls (and perhaps PROC
NLIN) care to shed some light results ?  Again, I am not so much frustrated
at the behavior of nls (it is what I would have expected with these data),
but rather curious as to why NLIN converged when nls didn't.  Thanks for any
explanation you could provide.

2) In fitting the above models my colleague chose to model percent of
initial remaining, hence the first data point is defined to be 100%.  All
other data points are calculated relative to the first.  He also would like
to force the models through an intercept of 100 at time zero. But, is it
appropriate to include the first data point (100%) in the model in this case
?  Since this point is defined to be 100 and defined to be on the line the
residual for this point is consequently defined to be zero, a violation of
the assumption of equal variances for the residual.  Can someone point me to
a reference which might address this issue or offer advice of their own.
I'm not sure if this is real cause for concern or if it is something which
in practice may be ignored.  The small size of the data sets makes me a
little nervous here.

Thanks again for any help and guidance this list may provide.  I will
summarize for the group.

Peter Scherer
Dow AgroSciences
Indianapolis, Indiana

messages.subject: Re: [S] summary:uncertainities from ratios
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Don MacQueen, Jim Pratt, Ray Falk, Dave Krantz, and
John Maindonal for replying my question and the citations.

Attached, the summary of Dave Krantz and John Maindonal replies.

Thanks,

Mario

-------------Original Question-----------------------

I have a probably simple question: I want to calculate the
uncertainties propagated from the uncertainties of concentrations, say
into two different media. For example, suppose that I have measured 4
times the element Be in a homogenous glass giving me 1.81 ppm of this
element and +- 0.11(2sigmas). The same element (Be) was measured 3
times in another phase (a mineral) with 1.60 (+- 0.33). I calculate the ratio
mineral/glass, which is 0.88, but how about the uncertainties here?

 --------------Reply from Dave Krantz----------------------

What is the relation between the standard errors of A, B,
and that of the ratio A/B?

The Taylor series for  R = A/B,  through its first two orders,
looks like this:

dR ~ (1/B)*dA - (A/B^2)*dB + (A/B^3)*dB^2 - (1/B^2)*dA*dB       (EQ 1)

(there is no term for dA^2 since the second partial derivative of R
with respect to A is 0).
In the application here, dA and dB can be considered independent
random variables with mean 0 (departures of sample mean from population
mean for the two samples--it is important that the samples are
independent, of course).

If one squares EQ 1, takes expectations, uses independence and mean 0,
and simplifies, one gets the following second-order approximation,
in which cvA, cvB, and cvR denote the coefficients of variation
of A, B, and R, B3 denotes the normalized third central moment
of the denominator B (expectation of the third power of the deviation
from the mean, divided by the third power of the mean), and B4 denotes
the analogous normalized fourth central moment of B:

cvR ~ sqrt(cvA^2 + cvB^2 + (cvA*cvB)^2 - 2*B3 + B4)             (EQ 2)

If the central limit theorem applies approximately to statistic B,
so its distribution is approximately Gaussian, EQ 2 can be simplified:
B3 is essentially 0 and B4 is approximately 3*(cvB^4).  So for this case,
the second-order approximation becomes

cvR ~ sqrt(cvA^2 + cvB^2 + (cvA*cvB)^2 + 3*(cvB^4))             (EQ 3)

If cvA and cvB are less than 20%, this is a quite good approximation;
and if they are less than 10%, the latter two terms in it play little
role--the first order approximation, essentially Pythagorean combination
of coefficients of variation is pretty good.  However, this second-order
approximation goes to pot rapidly for coefficients of variation
over 20%--one needs higher terms of the Taylor expansion and it
may no longer be worthwhile to look for any formula unless you have
particularly interesting special cases.

---------------------Comment from John Maindonald-----------------

Note also the simplified version of this formula, but allowing
for correlation between A and B:

  var[R] = 1/B^2(R^2 V22 - 2 R V12 +V11)

where var[A]=V11, var[B]=V22, cov[A,B]=V12.

Note also that an exact confidence interval is available for R.
I have code somewhere that calculates this. References are
Fieller, E. C. 1944.  Quart. J. Pharm. 17:117-123
Finney, D.J. 2ed, 1964.  Statistical Methods in Biological Assay
  (Griffin, London.)
Finney, D.J. 1971. Probit Analysis. Cambridge Univ Press.  (pp.78-80)

messages.subject: Re: [S] Sampling correlated vectors
messages.body_plain:
Rolf: 

Shades of the "Problem of Moments" (circa 1800,s by Chebyshev)

With a univariate sample it is perhaps easy to see that the standard
bootstrap is equivalent to estimating a distribution function that is
discrete and matches the first 2 * n -1 moments of the sample and then
sampling with replacement from it (assuming all values are unique you get
the distribution of p(Xi) = 1/n for all Xi, 0 otherwise). 

The same is true for multivariate samples. If computationally feasible the
original poster could create distributions that had the same first few
moments (including correlation) and (randomly) vary (consistent) higher
moments. 
(If anyone is really interested I'll post references and software leads to
do this sort of thing).

As an aside, in the mid-80,s I always wondered why the bootstrap was
considered "good" when at the same time the method of moments estimation was
consider "bad" when from this perspective they are mathematically identical.

Hope this is of some interest,

Keith O'Rourke
Statistician, Department of Surgery and Clinical Epidemiology Unit
University of Ottawa/ Ottawa Hospital

messages.subject: Re: [S] SAS does; S-Plus doesn't
messages.body_plain:
"Scherer, Peter" <pscherer at dowagro.com> writes:

> I have two issues which I encountered while modeling some soil degradation
> data.  The first related to nls and why S-Plus doesn't converge when SAS
> PROC NLIN does.  The second issue is, perhaps, a more philosophical question
> related to setting intercepts.
> 
> 1)  I have about twenty data sets of soil degradation data, each with 5 to
> 10 data points.  The response is percent remaining where the response has
> been scaled such that at time zero 100% remains and covariate is days .
> Some of the degradation curves exhibit classic first-order decay patterns of
> roughly exponential decline.  Others exhibit nearly linear decay patterns.
> To each data set I have been fitting a series of possible models, including
> exponential and biexponential models.  Three of the data sets in question
> are presented below.
> 
> # linear profile
> days.1 <- c(0,28,56,84,161)
> pct.1 <- c(100,64.89,59.19,48.71,23.90)
> # linear profile
> days.2 <- c(0,7,14,21,30,43)
> pct.2 <- c(100,81.8,67.9,69.2,40,8.61)
> # exponential decline
> days.3 <- c(0,3,7,14,21,28,56,129,224,357)
> pct.3 <- c(100,67.76,74.59,55.09,35.1,24.38,15.11,5.85,3.41,2.44)
> 
> # modeling statements for 3-parameter biexponential model, intercept forced
> through 100 at days=0
> ex1.nls <- nls(pct.1 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.1) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.1),
> trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005),nls.control(minscale=.0001,maxiter=100
> ,tolerance=.1))
> ex2.nls <- nls(pct.2 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.2) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.2),
> trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005),nls.control(minscale=.0001,maxiter=100
> ,tolerance=.1))
> ex3.nls <- nls(pct.3 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.3) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.3),
> trace=T,start=c(c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005))
> 
> [Note that the error messages for the first two models differ.  exp1.nls
> fails with "singular gradient matrix" (understandable) and exp2.nls fails
> with "step factor reduced below minimum".]
> 
> 
>  I was not surprised to find that nls did not converge on the first two
> sets, since to model this rather linear data using a biexponential model is
> to invite problems.  However, I was somewhat surprised to find that SAS's
> PROC NLIN did fit these models without difficulty.  Since this is an
> academic exercise and not an analysis for a client I am not overly
> concerned.  Still, I do find it disturbing that a colleague with essentially
> no experience with nonlinear models can code an inappropriate model into SAS
> and get convergence whereas I, using S-Plus and the same model description
> and starting values (simply double-checking his results), fail to get
> convergence.  Would someone with more experience using nls (and perhaps PROC
> NLIN) care to shed some light results ?  Again, I am not so much frustrated
> at the behavior of nls (it is what I would have expected with these data),
> but rather curious as to why NLIN converged when nls didn't.  Thanks for any
> explanation you could provide.

Could you give us more detail on how PROC NLIN was run?  I tried to
fit the first example using something simple like
 data days1;
     input days1 pct1;
     datalines;
     0 100.00
    28  64.89
    56  59.19
    84  48.71
   161  23.90
 ;

 proc nlin;
  parms c1=80,k1=.04,k2=.005;
  model pct1 = c1*exp(-k1*days1) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days1);
  run;

and got a note in the log file
NOTE: PROC NLIN grid search time was  0: 0: 0.
WARNING: PROC NLIN failed to converge.
NOTE: The PROCEDURE NLIN printed pages 1-4.

The end of the iteration output in the listing file is
  100     22.0139     0.00767      0.0106       158.8
so the best residual sum of squares is 158.8

Fitting a model with only one rate constant in S-PLUS (actually I used R but
the results should be similar) and imposing the constraint that pct is
100 at days = 0 I get

> ex1.nls <- nls(pct.1 ~ 100*exp(-exp(lrc)*days.1),
+ trace=T,start=c(lrc = -2.0), control = nls.control(maxiter=100,tol=.1))
10363.57 :  -2 
3637.546 :  -5.807627 
523.6241 :  -4.333968 
158.3558 :  -4.630713 
> exp(-4.630713)
[1] 0.009747806

so the SAS output is quite right, the three-parameter fit has not
converged.  A one-parameter model gives a better fit.

If you try to extend to the three-parameter model from the
one-parameter fit, you still run into problems using nls.

> ex1.nls <- nls(pct.1 ~ c1*exp(-k1*days.1) + (100-c1)*exp(-k2*days.1),
+ trace=T,start=c(c1=10,k1=.00005,k2=.0097),nls.control(maxiter=100,tol=.1))
222.0052 :  1.0e+01 5.0e-05 9.7e-03 
152.1766 :  24.545518078  0.005021563  0.010856898 
147.1008 :  44.101065016  0.006895463  0.011806955 
Error in nls(pct.1 ~ c1 * exp(-k1 * days.1) + (100 - c1) * exp(-k2 * days.1),  
: 
        step factor reduced below minimum

SAS PROC NLIN does better at this point but at the expense of changing
the model.  If you start PROC NLIN from the same starting values, it
converges in 25 iterations but warns you that the approximate Hessian
is singular (similar to the warning from nls of a singular gradient
matrix).

The converged value is
   26     82.4698     0.00691     35040.4     36.4103

Notice that the estimate of k2 is 35040.  Hence the term
exp(-k2*days.1) is a step function. It is one at days.1 = 0 and
zero for positive days.1

That model is trivial to fit if you recognize that all you are doing
is using a single exponential, dropping the point at days = 0 and
allowing the premultiplier to be free rather than fixed at 100.
> nls(pct.1 ~ exp(-exp(lk1) * days.1), start = c(lk1 = -4.6), alg = "plinear",
+     subset = days.1 > 0)  # this would look slightly different in S-PLUS
Nonlinear regression model
  model:  pct.1 ~ exp(-exp(lk1) * days.1) 
   data:  list 
      lk1      .lin 
-4.974881 82.469822 
 residual sum-of-squares:  36.41032 

Often people say that "NLIN converged" because it gave them output,
summaries, etc.  You have to be careful to check whether it really did
converge because it will give the summaries whether it has converged
or not.  Also, as mentioned on this list in the past, Bruce McCullogh
in his paper on "Experience with the StRD: Application and
Interpretation" compared several major statistical software packages'
nonlinear least squares routines on the NIST standard test problems
and noted:
 The StRD has been applied both formally and informally to over a
 dozen of the most popular statistics and econometrics packages, and
 only two of them have not produced nonlinear "solutions" with zero
 digits of accuracy: the statistical package S-PLUS (with analytic
 derivatives) and the econometrics package TSP (which has automatic
 analytic differentiation"

It is a mistake to think that there are parameter estimates for every
nonlinear model applied to every set of data.  Sometimes it is best to
find out that there are no reasonable parameter estimates.

> 2) In fitting the above models my colleague chose to model percent of
> initial remaining, hence the first data point is defined to be 100%.  All
> other data points are calculated relative to the first.  He also would like
> to force the models through an intercept of 100 at time zero. But, is it
> appropriate to include the first data point (100%) in the model in this case?

No.  If the first data point will always be (0, 100) and your model is
constrained to go through (0, 100) then you will not be adding any
information to the fit by including the point.  You will, however, be
artificially inflating the degrees of freedom for residuals which can
be important in cases like those above.  If you were able to fit the
three-parameter model you would calculate (5 - 3) = 2 degrees of
freedom for residuals whereas it should be (4 - 3) = 1.

I hope this helps.  I would be happy to continue a dialog on this,
perhaps in private e-mail so as not to clutter the list.
-- 
Douglas Bates                            bates at stat.wisc.edu
Statistics Department                    608/262-2598
University of Wisconsin - Madison        http://www.stat.wisc.edu/~bates/

messages.subject: Re: [S] Inverting non-square matrices
messages.body_plain:
At 14:23 07/09/00 -0700, Alexander Gershunov wrote:
>
>Dear Splusers,
>
>Could someone point me in the direction of an Splus function to compute 
>left and right inverses of rectangular matrices? 

ginverse(x) will calculate a left inverse of x (if one exists).
t(ginverse(t(x))) will calculate a right inverse of x (if one exists).

There is a terminology question here I may not be clear about, but I would
have said a left inverse exists if and only if x has full column rank.  In
this case you could also calculate it as solve(crossprod(x),t(x)).
Similarly if x has full row rank the right inverse is
t(x)%*%solve(crossprod(x))

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: More on Re: [S] SAS does; S-Plus doesn't
messages.subject_clean: More on Re: [S] SAS does; S-Plus doesn't
messages.body_plain:
This is a follow-up to an earlier thread on S-news following some
private e-mail exchanges with Peter Scherer and Devanarayan Viswanath.

The lesson here is that, for some programs, "has declared convergence"
is different from "has converged".

DEVANARAYAN_VISWANATH at Lilly.com writes:

> Thanks for posting your reply to the S-news group. I have often struggled
> getting the nls function to converge for some challenging dose-response
> curves, but have been able to get PROC NLIN, JMP, etc,  converge. The
> standard error message I often get from nls for most non-convergence cases
> is "step factor reduced below minimum". I have tried relaxing the control
> parameters in nls.control, but to no avail. Is this because nls has only
> two methods built in (newton-raphson and p-linear) whereas SAS and some
> other packages offer more options such as Marquardt?

The question is "What do you mean by convergence?".  In a private
message Peter sent me the code that his colleague had used for SAS
PROC NLIN.  If you go back and check the data the first of the days
vectors (days.1) is c(0, 28, 56, 84, 161).  The converged value from
PROC NLIN gives a warning that the approximate Hessian matrix is
singular but it still prints out the estimates as
                            Asymptotic
                              Standard
 Parameter      Estimate         Error    Asymptotic 95% Confidence Limits

 XS              17.5302        5.2529      0.8127     34.2477
 K1                299.3        Infty      -Infty       Infty 
 K3              0.00691      0.000952     0.00388     0.00994

Look at that estimate for K1.  Does that look as if it has converged?

Essentially what has happened is that the model has collapsed.  That
estimate of k1 should be infinity and any large, positive value will
give exactly the same sum-of-squares, fitted values, etc. because K1
enters the model in a term like exp(-K1 * days.1).  When days.1 = 0,
this evaluates to 1 and when days.1 >= 28, it is essentially zero.
Stating that the estimate is 299.3 is arbitrary.  I would claim that
this procedure has not "converged".

The nls function in S-PLUS does not declare convergence in such a
situation.  When the gradient matrix becomes computational singular it
reports this and stops.  It is then up to the analyst to examine the
behavior of the iterations and see if it was just a poor choice of
starting estimates or if in fact this means that the model doesn't fit
the data.

This is more in keeping with the S-PLUS philosophy of data analysis
where the user is expected to be interacting with the data, not just
running canned analyses on it.

> I am not sure I understand the implication of the statement "only two of
> them have not produced nonlinear "solutions" with zero digits of accuracy"
> in the following quote from Bruce McCullogh. Could you please shed some
> light on this? Do you happen to know where and when his paper was
> published?
>  The StRD has been applied both formally and informally to over a
>  dozen of the most popular statistics and econometrics packages, and
>  only two of them have not produced nonlinear "solutions" with zero
>  digits of accuracy: the statistical package S-PLUS (with analytic
>  derivatives) and the econometrics package TSP (which has automatic
>  analytic differentiation"

Bruce McCullogh is talking about situations like this where the
nonlinear least squares algorithms in other packages just declare
convergence and stop.  In the examples from NIST that he uses (the
so-called StRD) there are "certified" solutions.  McCullough found
that all the packages except S-PLUS and TSP declared convergence
falsely at least once during the testing.  Part of his testing is to
check the number of digits to which the solution from the package
matches the certified solution.  If they differ on the first digit of
the answer he says that is a false convergence.

I guess the point that I would like to make is that the good property
of nls is that it uses a reliable convergence criterion so when nls
has converged you have a reasonable assurance that you are at a local
minimum of the residual sum-of-squares surface and within reasonable
parameter regions.  For other packages the fact that they _declare
convergence_ does not always mean that they have converged.

Disclaimer:  I am one of the original authors of the nls function so I
am not exactly a disinterested observer.

-- 
Douglas Bates                            bates at stat.wisc.edu
Statistics Department                    608/262-2598
University of Wisconsin - Madison        http://www.stat.wisc.edu/~bates/

messages.subject: Re: [S] random factors in anova
messages.body_plain:
> From: aczarn at cs.uwa.edu.au
> Date: Fri, 8 Sep 2000 16:51:35 +0800
> 
> i am doing some anova analysis at the moment.
> 
> the factors in my analysis are random factors.
> what i want to be able to do is to say which
> factors are significant.
> 
> unfortunately, when i use the random anova in splus,
> ie raov, the summary command does not generate

That's only one of many ways. aov itself can have Error terms, 
varcomp can analyse nested random effects, and lme can do all
of this and more (or at least in nlme3 it can, in S-PLUS 2000 and
available at nlme.stat.wisc.edu for other versions).

> p values for the factors themselves.

I'm not sure I understand.  First, a factor marked as random is being
regarded as a sample from a population, and any inference applies to
variance components in the population, not the factor (S-PLUS sense).
Second, as what one observes are combinations of variance components,
inference on one variance component may depend critically on which
others are assumed to be non-zero.

Here's a way to do the raov/varcomp help example via lme.

summary(lme(Moisture ~ 1, random=~ 1 | Batch/Sample,  data=pigment))

Now suppse you want to test if the Sample var component is significantly
non-zero via REML:

fit1 <- lme(Moisture ~ 1, random=~ 1 | Batch/Sample,  data=pigment)
fit2 <- lme(Moisture ~ 1, random=~ 1 | Batch,  data=pigment)
anova(fit2, fit1)
    Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value 
fit2     1  3 374.6406 380.8732 -184.3203                        
fit1     2  4 300.2623 308.5725 -146.1312 1 vs 2 76.37825  <.0001

which is valid (since we have not changed the fixed effects) in
asymptotic theory.

Again, I am not sure why you would want to do this.  If an effect
is intended to be random, that's a design consideration and normally
one would keep it random in the analysis.  In my experience whether
variance components are regarded as significant is a practical not
statistical issue.

> if there any way i can get around this ??? for exmaple
> in gam, once can specify factors to be random using
> the random function viz
> gam(y ~ random(f1) + random(f2, df = 3) + x)

Eh?  You can do that, but it gives you a shrunked smoother, not a
random-effects anova.  I think its title is rather misleading.
The analogue for aov is Error, which does give you a random-effects
anova, but no tests.

> is there anyway i can do this in anova in splus and
> get p values for the factors themselves ???
> 
> a colleague suggested using REML, but i see no
> implementation of REML in Splus.

Well, that's like EM, a principle not a method, but even so I'm
surprised you failed to find mention of it. (Try the index of V&R3!)
lme uses REML by default, varcomp has a REML method and raov is in fact
using REML, for example, since in balanced setups the method of moments
estimators coincide with REML.

--

messages.body_plain:
> Date: Fri, 08 Sep 2000 03:59:21 -0700
> From: " Clark Sims " <clarksimssplus at my-deja.com>
> 
> 
>  Is there a command in S+ analogous to the C++ code:
> try {
>   .....
> } catch (...) {
> 
> }

Yes, it's called try()!   There is an earlier function called restart
that should only be used with great care. If your version of S+
does not have try (2000 and 5.1 do), there is an emulation on page 48
of V&R's `S Programming'.

> I am doing some long loops and it would be nice to be able to skip the cases 
which cause error conditions.

That's what try/restart are for.

> Has anybody tried masking the stop command? If I mask the stop command, 
> should 
this handle all normal error conditions (ie. error which don't cause S+ to 
crash)

No error should cause S+ to crash!  Masking the stop *function* will
not do anything about the C code (system or user) that calls the error
handler.  It's much safer to use try().

messages.subject: [S] Simulating from a quasi likelihood GLM
messages.subject_clean: [S] Simulating from a quasi likelihood GLM
messages.body_plain:
Can anyone shed some light on the following problem, or know of papers on
simulating from GLMs, particularly using quasi-likelihood?

I have fitted a GLM using quasi likelihood with the variance proportional to
the mean and a log link.  I now want to simulate forecasts, taking account
of estimation error and process error, where

process variance=scale parameter * mean
estimation variance=mean^2*variance(linear predictor)     ' since I am using
a log link
prediction error=(process variance+estimation variance)^0.5

The GLM gives parameter estimates (b) and a covariance matrix (V) of
parameter estimates.  From these, the forecast "means" are obtained by
exponentiating the linear predictors.  I can also obtain the s.d. of the
forecast linear predictors using predict.glm(newdata, se.fit=T,
type="link"), and the s.d. (standard error) of the fitted means using
predict.glm(newdata, se.fit=T, type="response")

I am simulating using a two step procedure:

1) estimation error: simulate the "mean" forecasts from a distribution for
the mean with expected value equal to the forecast mean, and variance
provided using predict.glm(newdata, se.fit=T, type="response"),

2) process error: given each simulated mean, simulate a forecast observation
from a distribution with variance proportional to that simulated mean, where
the constant of proportionality is provided by the scale parameter from the
GLM.

I am simulating using a log-normal distribution for step 1 (with parameters
chosen to replicate the target mean and sd).  This is to ensure that the
mean is always positive.  I am then simulating from a gamma distribution
with parameters alpha, beta such that alpha=simulated mean/scale,
beta=scale.

Obviously, the gamma distribution at stage two requires a positive simulated
mean, hence log-normal at step 1.

The resulting simulations have the desired average, with sd equal to the
prediction error, as required.

My questions are:

1) Is the two step procedure valid?
2) Is the lognormal/gamma implementation sensible?

On question 2, I vaguely recollect that linear predictors are asymptotically
normal, so in step 1 the linear predictors could be simulated as
multivariate normal (b, V), then exponentiated.  This would target the
correct average linear predictor (lp), but would bias the simulated forecast
mean which would have expected value exp(lp+0.5*var(lp)).

I also recollect that means tend to normality, via the CLT.  So it might be
better to simulate the forecast means using a normal distribution with
mean=exp(lp) and variance given by the estimation variance.  This would
allow a negative mean requiring an alternative to the gamma at stage 2.

(Note: I cannot go straight to the predictive distribution since I also need
to take account of correlations between forecast values induced by the
parameterisation.  This can be done at step 1 after simulating the means)

Any thoughts?

Thanks in advance,

Peter.

messages.subject: [S] test whether a density is unimodal
messages.subject_clean: [S] test whether a density is unimodal
messages.body_plain:
There is something called the coefficient of bimodality. It the following
ratio: (1+skewness^2)/(kurtosis+3) where the "kurtosis" vanishes for the
normal.

This coefficient has value .555 for the uniform, and 1 (exactly) for the
Bernoulli distribution. The Bernoulli of course has only two values with
prob p and 1-p, the ultimate bimodal. I don't know any additional
properties. The sampling version of the coefficient is defined slightly
differently to avoid bias for small samples.

Another approach would be to use cross-entropy between the data and a two
parametric forms, one unimodal and the other multimodal. Say a normal with
unknown mean and variance (two free parameters) and the other a mixture of
normals (as many as 5 parameters). Then use the EM algorithm to get the
cross-entropy from the expect log likelihood. The details are a little
tricky. I think in general this is a hard problem.
